recurringPatterns.pattern: The evidentiary concession-then-assertion: a source is credited, then denied the larger claim, in a fixed two- or three-sentence shape. Used dozens of times per chapter until it reads as a template rather than a judgment.
instances: The site does not prove that warfare had one origin, nor that every community of the same period lived under similar threat. It shows that organised or repeated group violence appeared in at least some early settings
Jericho’s construction shows preparedness and collective effort; it does not supply a calendar of assaults.

recurringPatterns.pattern: Symmetrical paired antithesis as paragraph closer — “It could A. It could also B.” — hedging in a balanced couplet rather than adjudicating.
instances: Familiarity can restrain violence because reputation has time to accumulate. It can also sharpen resentment because debts and insults are remembered in the place where they occurred.
The same dossier could protect a person by establishing status and expose that person by marking difference.

recurringPatterns.pattern: The two-case comparison scaffold: two sites/institutions introduced separately, compared in a “The difference is not that…” or “The contrast can be stated plainly” paragraph, then a verdict paragraph. Every chapter runs this same machine, so chapter shapes become interchangeable.
instances: The contrast can be stated plainly. Çatalhöyük concentrates resources inside households. Jericho concentrates labour around a shared boundary.
The verdict is limited but clear. Ottoman organisation gave the central government a durable infantry core and strong artillery traditions for siege warfare.

recurringPatterns.pattern: The enumerated inventory sentence — a long comma-chain of sites, objects or offices standing in for analysis, usually opening or closing a section.
instances: the sixty-one individuals at Jebel Sahaba in the Nile Valley; projectile fragments lodged among their bones; healed injuries that indicate survival before the final episode; unhealed wounds…

Andean terraces, where shared repair can become tribute; Californian oak groves, where seasonal abundance supports storage and inherited rights; Dutch polders, where common defence depends on unequal payments and votes

recurringPatterns.pattern: Cross-chapter redundancy: the same case is re-introduced from scratch in a later chapter, repeating dates, figures and framing already given.
instances: The people buried there lived roughly between 13,400 and 18,600 years ago, according to the dating associated with the site.
The cemetery in the Nile Valley, dated broadly to between about 13,400 and 18,600 years ago, contains sixty-one individuals

summary: This is a serious, evidence-first world history of organised aggression, held together by a real and unusually well-sustained thesis: that each class of source (bone, chronicle, law, demography, testimony) licenses only certain claims, and that human dispositions become raids, sieges, drafts or deportations only when institutions supply means, targets and permission. The reasoning is disciplined, the specificity is high and largely accurate in texture, and the prose is clean, unhurried, and free of the usual lexical slop — no stock pivots, no motivational filler, few dead abstractions. What weakens it is shape rather than substance. The same rhetorical machine runs in every chapter — case, counter-case, “this shows X but not Y,” balanced antithesis, verdict — until paragraphs become predictable at the level of form even when their content is fresh, and chapters end where the machine stops rather than where the argument lands. Pacing suffers most: Chapters 2, 5 and 8 accumulate inventories and near-duplicate comparisons, several cases (Jebel Sahaba, Saint-Domingue, Njals saga, Ashoka) are re-introduced from scratch later, and one paragraph summarising the medieval chapter has been stranded under the Chapter 8 heading. Cut the redundant re-introductions, vary the paragraph architecture, and let more sections end without a two-beat aphorism, and this would be close to publishable non-fiction.
